issues.subcategory: contradictory effect size values across sections
issues.description: The original study's effect size for 'Advantageous' self-disclosure is reported inconsistently across sections. In the abstract it is stated as -.30, in the Results section it is compared against -.30, but in Table 3 the original r is listed as -.33, and in the Discussion it is referenced as -.33. This inconsistency undermines confidence in the accuracy of the reported values and the difference calculations in Table 3.
issues.quote: self-esteem only weakly and inconsistently predicted perceived advantages of self-disclosure on Facebook (meta analytic effect size = -.16, original effect size = -.30)... The effect sizes of all studies were descriptively less than or equal to the original (-.02 to -.30 vs. -.30)... [Table 3 shows original r = -0.33 for Advantageous]

issues.subcategory: contradictory prediction interval values across sections
issues.description: The prediction interval for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' meta-analytic effect is reported as [-.09, .26] in the Results section but as [-.07, .27] in the Discussion section. These are not the same values, indicating a transcription or calculation error in one of the sections.
issues.quote: Results: 95% PI [-.09, .26]... Discussion: supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.

issues.subcategory: contradictory fail-safe number values
issues.description: The fail-safe number (FSN) for the 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' outcome is reported as 5 in the Results section but as 11 in the Discussion section. These are materially different values that lead to different substantive conclusions about the stability of the finding.
issues.quote: Results: The FSN was 5 studies... Discussion: These findings also seemed somewhat unstable, as shown by the low FSN (11 studies).

issues.subcategory: sign direction inconsistency for connect outcome
issues.description: The meta-analytic effect size for 'Opportunity to Connect with Others' is reported as .09 (positive) in the Discussion, but the original study found a negative effect (-.22), and the authors state that 'the summary estimate of the effect size was opposite in direction to the original in six of the seven replications.' If most replications are positive and the meta-analytic estimate is positive (.09), the direction is opposite to the original (negative), which is internally consistent, but the authors then say the meta-analytic effect size 'was .09, and significantly different from zero' while also saying the PI includes zero and future studies are unlikely to find the effect — these claims are in tension.
issues.quote: the meta-analytic effect size was .09, and significantly different from zero. We believe that it will be unlikely that future studies will find an effect similar to the original, supported by the 95% PI of [-.07, .27], which includes zero.

issues.subcategory: incorrect equivalence of beta and r
issues.description: The authors state 'Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient' in the Table 1 note. This is only true in simple bivariate regression with a single predictor and no covariates. While the original study appears to use simple regression, this equivalence claim is technically imprecise and potentially misleading. Standardized beta from OLS regression equals r only in the bivariate case; any deviation (e.g., inclusion of covariates) would invalidate this equivalence. The authors do not confirm that all regressions were strictly bivariate.
issues.quote: Note. Beta coefficients are standardized (consistent with the original research). Effect size r is equivalent to the beta coefficient.

issues.subcategory: misinterpretation of prediction interval for expression outcome
issues.description: The authors state the PI for 'Opportunity to Express Self' is [.01, .14] and conclude this means 'future studies would find an effect size between .01 and .14 (smaller than the original).' However, a prediction interval represents where 95% of future single-study effect sizes are expected to fall, not a guarantee. More critically, the PI lower bound of .01 barely excludes zero, yet the authors use this to argue for a small positive effect while simultaneously arguing the FSN of only 3 studies means they are 'confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect.' These two conclusions are contradictory.
issues.quote: the PI [.01, .14] showed that 95% of future studies would find an effect size between .01 and .14 (smaller than the original)... The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant, led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: FSN misreported for expression outcome
issues.description: In the Results section, the FSN for 'Opportunity to Express Self' is reported as 3, but in the Discussion it is described as 'only five unreported studies.' This is an internal inconsistency in the FSN value for the same outcome variable.
issues.quote: Results: The FSN was 3 studies... Discussion: The FSN analysis, which indicated that only five unreported studies could reduce the results of the meta-analytic effect size p-value to nonsignificant

issues.subcategory: contradictory characterization of expression outcome significance
issues.description: For the 'Opportunity to Express Self' outcome, the authors state 'all individual replications found regression coefficients not significantly different from zero,' yet also report that 'the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero.' The authors then conclude in the Discussion that they are 'confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect.' This is contradictory: the meta-analytic result is statistically significant (p=.021), yet the authors conclude there is no effect.
issues.quote: Even though the effect size meta-analysis revealed that the point-estimate meta-analytic effect size of the seven replication studies, r = .08, p = .021, was statistically different from zero... led us to be confident that future replications would find the same lack of an effect as our replications.

issues.subcategory: missing original beta coefficient for expression outcome
issues.description: The original study's beta coefficient for 'Opportunity to Express Self' is listed as 'n/a' in Table 1, with only a p-value (.181) reported. The authors note 'The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable.' This means the effect size r for the original study on this outcome cannot be directly compared, yet the authors proceed to compare replication effect sizes to an original effect size of .15 (mentioned in the Results). The source and calculation of this .15 value is not explained.
issues.quote: * The original study did not report a beta coefficient for this variable... Five of the seven studies showed an effect size descriptively smaller than the original study (.06 to .12 vs. .15)

issues.subcategory: missing details on composite score calculation inconsistency
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed' rather than mean-averaged as in other studies, but do not report whether this was corrected before analysis or how it affected the results. This is a potentially serious methodological inconsistency that could inflate or deflate effect sizes for the Gordon replication, yet no correction or sensitivity analysis is reported.
issues.quote: Two studies included analysis scripts that showed scores for all scales were mean averaged. The means for scores in most studies implied that the items were mean averaged, but the Gordon study's mean implied items were summed.

issues.subcategory: missing information on missing data handling
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.' but do not report what was done to address this in the meta-analysis. The impact of potentially different missing data handling procedures across studies on the meta-analytic results is unaddressed.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent measurement scale across replications
issues.description: Two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale while all others used the original four-point scale. This is a meaningful measurement difference that could affect the distribution and variance of the predictor variable, and consequently the regression coefficients and effect sizes. The authors acknowledge this but do not conduct any sensitivity analysis excluding these studies or statistically test whether scale format moderates results.
issues.quote: most replications used the original four-point scale, while two replications (IIT-Sp16 and IIT-Sp17) used a five-point scale.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent data collection mode across replications
issues.description: Replications used different data collection modes (in-lab only, online only, or both), which is a known moderator of self-report responses, particularly for sensitive items related to self-esteem and social media use. Three replications used in-lab only, two used online only, and two used both. This confound is acknowledged but not analyzed as a moderator, and the mixed-mode studies introduce within-study heterogeneity that is not addressed.
issues.quote: researchers employed both methods (three replications had participants complete in lab only, two used online only, and two used both methods).

issues.subcategory: group administration in one replication
issues.description: The SAU replication ran participants in groups of two to six, while all other replications ran participants individually. Group administration can introduce social desirability effects and demand characteristics, particularly for self-esteem measures and perceptions of social media. This is a direct violation of the original study's individual administration protocol and could systematically bias results from this site.
issues.quote: Participants completing questionnaires in the lab did so alone, except for the SAU replication, which ran participants in groups of two to six.

issues.subcategory: inadequate minimum sample size for replication goals
issues.description: The minimum sample size was set at 120, yet two replications (Gordon: N=80, BYU-Sp16: N=90) fall below this threshold. The authors state 'All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study),' which is directly contradicted by the data in Table 1. This raises questions about inclusion criteria consistency.
issues.quote: All studies in this meta-analysis received this approval by the CREP team, collected the minimum number of participants specified by the CREP (120 for the present study to ensure adequate statistical power)... [Table 1: Gordon N=80, BYU-Sp16 N=90]

issues.subcategory: item wording differences in predictor measure
issues.description: One replication (IIT-Sp16) had 'slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items' of the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale. Changing four of ten items (40% of the scale) is a substantial modification that could affect construct validity of the self-esteem measure. No psychometric comparison between the modified and standard scale is provided, and no sensitivity analysis excluding this study is reported.
issues.quote: one study (IIT-Sp16) had slight differences in item order and in wording on four out of ten items (e.g., 'At times I think I am no good at all' vs. 'I think I am no good at all')

issues.subcategory: exclusive use of undergraduate student samples
issues.description: All seven replications used undergraduate student samples, as did the original study. The authors do not adequately address the limitation that findings may not generalize to the broader population of Facebook users, which includes two billion people worldwide as cited in the introduction. The discussion of generalizability focuses on cross-cultural differences but does not address the fundamental age and education homogeneity of the samples.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US... Among social network sites, Facebook is a dominant platform that affects the thinking, emotions, behavior, and interactions of its active users, some two billion people worldwide

issues.subcategory: all samples from US institutions only
issues.description: All seven replications were conducted at US institutions, yet the authors discuss implications for social compensation theory broadly and make comparisons to Turkish samples. The geographic restriction to the US is not adequately foregrounded as a limitation when drawing theoretical conclusions, and the authors' own discussion suggests cultural context may be a critical moderator.
issues.quote: Participants in all studies were undergraduate students at the five universities and colleges in the US... more collectivist cultures, like Turkey... may prompt people to use Facebook for different reasons than those in individualist cultures.

issues.subcategory: causal language from correlational/regression data
issues.description: The authors use causal and predictive language throughout (e.g., 'self-esteem predicts,' 'low self-esteem will feel safer') based on cross-sectional regression data. The original study and all replications are cross-sectional, meaning directionality cannot be established. It is equally plausible that perceptions of Facebook safety influence self-esteem, or that a third variable drives both.
issues.quote: We can conclude with some confidence that individuals with low self-esteem will feel safer self-disclosing on Facebook than in FTF interactions... Future studies seem likely to find that self-esteem would predict users' perception that Facebook was more advantageous for self-disclosure than FTF

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confounds in self-esteem and Facebook perception relationship
issues.description: The regression analyses do not control for potential confounds such as frequency of Facebook use, social anxiety, introversion/extraversion, or prior negative FTF social experiences. These variables could plausibly explain the relationship between self-esteem and Facebook perceptions. The original study's design limitations are replicated without improvement, and no discussion of these confounds is provided.
issues.quote: participants completed the 10-item Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (RSE; Rosenberg, 1965)... Next, participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers

issues.subcategory: Facebook perception measure not validated independently
issues.description: The Facebook perception measure was 'created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012)' and no independent psychometric validation is cited. The measure's factor structure, discriminant validity, and convergent validity are not established beyond internal consistency (alpha). The authors report alphas but do not address whether the subscales measure distinct constructs, particularly given the conceptual overlap between 'safety of self-disclosure' and 'advantages of self-disclosure.'
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012). Three items each assessed the degree to which participants believed Facebook enabled them to express themselves and to connect with others. Perceived safety of self-disclosure on Facebook compared to in person interactions was measured with nine items. Ten more items assessed perceived advantages of disclosing on Facebook versus FTF.

issues.subcategory: temporal validity of Facebook perception measure
issues.description: The Facebook perception measure was created in 2012 and used in replications conducted in 2016-2017. The authors themselves note significant shifts in social media usage patterns, with Instagram and Snapchat becoming dominant platforms for the college-age demographic. The measure's items may no longer have the same meaning or relevance to participants who primarily use other platforms, threatening construct validity across the temporal gap.
issues.quote: both Snapchat and Instagram were among a new crop of social media outlets for US and UK participants that challenged Facebook as the preferred social networking site for the age cohort of the participants in this research... self-expression was recently found to be a significant predictor of usage only on Instagram and Snapchat among college-aged participants

issues.subcategory: post-hoc model selection without pre-registration
issues.description: The authors report comparing REML and DerSimonian-Laird models and selecting REML because 'it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates.' This post-hoc model selection based on output interpretability rather than a priori theoretical or statistical justification represents an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom. It is unclear whether this choice was pre-registered or made after examining the data.
issues.quote: We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates for our data

issues.subcategory: selective inclusion of replication studies
issues.description: The CREP project page has 17 'forks' representing teams that started the replication process, but only 7 met inclusion criteria. The criteria for inclusion (minimum sample size, posted data and results) are described, but it is unclear whether teams that started but did not complete the study represent a form of selective attrition that could bias the meta-analytic results. Teams that found null results may have been less motivated to complete and post their data.
issues.quote: The Forest and Wood (2012) CREP replication project page on the OSF has 17 'forks' representing research teams or institutions that have started the replication process... These teams generated seven studies that met the minimum sample size, and posted data and results for the study in the OSF repository.

issues.subcategory: no reporting of participant exclusions within studies
issues.description: The authors do not report whether any participants were excluded from individual replication studies (e.g., for failing attention checks, not being Facebook users, incomplete responses). Given that the measure specifically asks about Facebook perceptions, participants who do not use Facebook would provide meaningless data. No information is provided about Facebook usage rates in the samples or exclusion of non-users.
issues.quote: not all studies posted analysis scripts or narratives to help us determine such things as missing data handling, composite score calculations, data exclusions, etc.

issues.subcategory: missing demographic data across studies
issues.description: Race data was only collected in three of seven replications, and the authors note 'in all other studies no other demographic information was collected.' This prevents any examination of whether sample demographic composition moderates effects, and limits the ability to assess whether samples are comparable across sites. The justification that the original study did not collect this information is insufficient for a replication meta-analysis seeking to understand moderators.
issues.quote: In three replications (BYU-Wi17, IIT-Sp16, and IIT-Sp17), race data was collected, but in all other studies no other demographic information was collected because the original Forest and Wood (2012) research did not indicate any other demographic information was collected

issues.subcategory: misapplication of social compensation theory
issues.description: The authors claim the results 'provide some support for social compensation theory' based on findings that low self-esteem individuals perceive Facebook as safer for self-disclosure. However, social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000) specifically predicts that socially anxious or lonely individuals will use online interactions to compensate for deficits in FTF relationships, leading to actual behavioral outcomes. The present study only measures perceptions of Facebook, not actual compensatory behavior or outcomes, making the theoretical claim an overclaim.
issues.quote: The present research also provides some support for social compensation theory (McKenna & Bargh, 2000; Wilson et al., 2012). This theory suggests that for those with lower self-esteem, the anxiety provoked by FTF interactions can be somewhat mitigated in online interactions.

issues.subcategory: publication bias inference from effect size attenuation is speculative
issues.description: The authors repeatedly infer publication bias in the original study from the observation that replication effect sizes are smaller than the original. While this pattern is consistent with publication bias, it is equally consistent with other explanations including regression to the mean (winner's curse), temporal changes in Facebook usage patterns, or genuine population differences. The authors do not conduct a formal publication bias test (e.g., Egger's test, funnel plot asymmetry) and conflate multiple possible explanations.
issues.quote: all factors indicating the presence of publication bias in the original study... the latter finding consistent with original study's larger susceptibility to publication bias than replication studies.

issues.subcategory: Table 2 content not provided
issues.description: Table 2 is referenced in the text as showing 'descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables,' but the table content is not included in the manuscript as provided. This prevents evaluation of sample comparability across sites and verification of the descriptive statistics referenced in the text.
issues.quote: Table 2 shows each study's descriptive statistics for gender, race, and the mean and standard deviation for self-esteem and each of the four outcome variables.

issues.subcategory: heterogeneity confidence intervals not interpretable without context
issues.description: The authors report very wide confidence intervals for I² (e.g., for Safety: 27.06% to 94.69%; for Expression: 0% to 79%) but do not discuss the implications of this uncertainty. With only 7 studies, these intervals are so wide as to be nearly uninformative, yet the authors draw conclusions about heterogeneity (e.g., 'showed some evidence of heterogeneity') without acknowledging that the CIs span from negligible to extreme heterogeneity.
issues.quote: The between-study variance showed some evidence of heterogeniety, Q(df = 6) = 18.69, p = 0.005; T2 = .02, 95% CI [0, .15]; I2 = 71.76%, 95% CI [27.06%, 94.69%].

issues.subcategory: no reporting of Facebook usage rates in samples
issues.description: The study measures perceptions of Facebook specifically, yet no information is provided about what proportion of participants in each replication were active Facebook users. If a substantial proportion of participants rarely or never use Facebook, their responses to the perception items would be uninformed guesses rather than genuine perceptions, introducing noise and potentially biasing results toward the null.
issues.quote: participants completed a measure of Facebook use perceptions created by the original researchers (Forest & Wood, 2012).

issues.subcategory: inconsistent description of original study's hypothesis and findings
issues.description: In the introduction, the authors describe Forest and Wood's hypothesis as predicting that 'people with low self-esteem would perceive Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose, and a better place to express their emotions with others.' However, the original study's Study 1 found no effect for self-expression, which the authors note. Yet the original study's beta for 'Express' is listed as positive (.15, p=.181) in Table 3, suggesting higher self-esteem was (non-significantly) associated with more perceived expression opportunity — opposite to the hypothesized direction. This directional inconsistency is not discussed.
issues.quote: Forest and Wood speculated that Facebook had benefits for people with low self-esteem... hypothesized that people with low self-esteem would perceive Facebook as a safer place to self-disclose, and a better place to express their emotions... [Table 3: original r for Express = 0.15, positive direction]

issues.subcategory: no pre-registration of meta-analytic protocol
issues.description: While individual replication studies were pre-registered, the meta-analytic protocol itself does not appear to have been pre-registered. Decisions about which studies to include, which effect size metric to use, which meta-analytic model to apply, and how to handle heterogeneity were made post-hoc. The preregistration badge claimed applies to individual studies, not to the meta-analysis itself.
issues.quote: This manuscript qualifies for a Preregistration badge; the data collection and data analysis methods were preregistered at each individual study's OSF page... We compared restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and DerSimonian and Laird (DL) models and selected REML as it produced more interpretable heterogeneity estimates

issues.subcategory: inappropriate use of fail-safe N as stability indicator
issues.description: The authors use the fail-safe number (FSN) as an indicator of result stability and robustness, but the FSN has been widely criticized as a flawed metric that does not adequately address publication bias and can be misleadingly large even for spurious effects. The authors do not acknowledge these limitations or supplement with more modern publication bias assessments (e.g., PET-PEESE, selection models, funnel plot asymmetry tests).
issues.quote: we conducted a fail-safe number (FSN) analysis (Rosenberg, 2005)... The FSN was 133 studies... These results also seemed to be somewhat robust, as indicated by a high FSN (133).

issues.subcategory: underpowered individual replication studies for effect size comparison goals
issues.description: The authors acknowledge that 'the sample sizes required for precision in comparing the difference in effect sizes will be larger than for judging simple significance,' yet most individual replications have sample sizes of 80-116, which are severely underpowered for detecting meaningful differences between replication and original effect sizes. This means the 95% CIs for effect size differences are very wide, and the failure to find significant differences between replications and the original cannot be interpreted as evidence of equivalence.
issues.quote: When comparing the effect sizes of the four outcome variables between the original study and the replication studies, we are constrained in our inference or conclusions by relatively wide CIs. This is primarily caused by the small sample size of the original study, as well as the rather small sample sizes of the replication studies.
